title: The Courtroom
victoryHeadline: Order! The court finds you correct on all counts.
acts: Day nine of the trial, and nobody in the building was thinking about the trial. Arthur had climbed down off the Judge's Bench entirely and was working through what he called his backswing, gavel in hand, on the theory that nine days behind a desk demanded some kind of exercise. Down in the Gallery, Benjamin stood at the end of a row of chairs with his arms folded, watching the one occupied seat in the room with the specific resentment of a man who had queued for two hours and lost it to someone who'd queued for six. Camila, in that seat, had a sketchbook open on her knee and no intention of noticing him. And over on the Prosecution carpet, Daisy paced her closing argument at a volume generally reserved for hailing ships, while Howard stood behind the potted plant a few feet away, rehearsing under his breath the testimony nobody had called him for yet.

It went on like that all afternoon. Camila's pencil moved faster than her eyes ever seemed to, sketching the glaring man at the end of the row in a style she suspected he'd hate. At the Witness Stand, Eliza reached the forty-minute mark of an answer that had stopped being about the case somewhere around minute twelve and become, instead, a full account of her sister's upcoming wedding, and nobody present had found the nerve to interrupt her. In Security, Graham had the monitors on in the background and a nature documentary in the foreground, three episodes deep into wildebeest migration and privately convinced this counted as multitasking. And at the far end of the Defense floor, Fritz ran a hand along the edge of the big oak table, admiring the joinery — he'd taken up furniture restoration that spring — while Vanessa stood with her back to the room at the other end, phone tucked inside a legal pad, quietly pricing flights for a trip she hadn't mentioned to the firm.

The crash, when it came, sounded like a wardrobe going down a lift shaft, and it landed underneath Daisy's closing argument so neatly that three people in Prosecution assumed it was a filing cabinet and one assumed it was Howard's nerves. By the time anyone thought to check the Defense area, Camila had already sketched Benjamin's expression at losing yet another objection, Eliza had finally reached the actual verb, Graham had seen his wildebeest cross the river, and Howard had, at long last, been called — for the wrong case, as it turned out, which he did not mention. Vanessa did not answer when the recess was announced. She never got up at all.

whereabouts.A: Arthur had climbed down off the Judge's Bench altogether, gavel in hand, working through what he privately called his backswing, on the theory that a courtroom is basically a nine-day desk job and a man needs exercise somewhere.
whereabouts.B: Benjamin stood at the end of a row of Gallery chairs, arms folded, keeping a wounded eye on the one seat in the room he considered rightfully his by seniority of queueing, currently occupied by someone else entirely.
whereabouts.C: Camila had the only occupied chair in the Gallery and a sketchbook open on her knee, quietly working on a caricature of the man glaring at her from the end of the row.
whereabouts.D: Daisy paced the Prosecution carpet end to end delivering her closing argument at a volume generally reserved for hailing ships, and had been told more than once that afternoon that she could be heard three rooms away.
whereabouts.E: Eliza, forty minutes into an answer at the Witness Stand, had somewhere around minute twelve stopped discussing the case and started recounting her sister's wedding plans in full, and nobody had yet found the nerve to stop her.
whereabouts.F: Fritz stood at the far end of the Defense table running a hand along its edge, quietly admiring the joinery — he'd taken up furniture restoration that spring, and noted with real professional interest that a table built this well weighed a good deal less than it looked.
whereabouts.G: Graham had the security monitors on in the background and his phone in his lap, three episodes deep into a documentary about wildebeest migration, on the theory that watching an empty hallway and learning something can technically happen at the same time.
whereabouts.H: Howard stood behind the potted plant in Prosecution rehearsing, under his breath, the testimony he'd been called to give about a boundary dispute eleven years old, hoping someone would remember to call him before evening.
whereabouts.V: Vanessa stood at the far end of the Defense floor with her back to the room, phone tucked inside a legal pad, quietly pricing flights for a holiday she hadn't mentioned to the firm yet.

reveal: It was Fritz, in the Defense area, with the table. Nine days as second chair had taught him exactly how much that table weighed and exactly how little anyone would question a young man everyone assumed was too junior to matter — including, in the end, Vanessa, who never turned around. He got both hands under the far edge and let the table finish an argument he'd stopped wanting to have with words. The crash was swallowed whole by a Prosecution closing argument three rooms over that half the building was already sick of, which is the only mercy anyone got that afternoon — nobody came running, and Fritz had time to put his hands back in his pockets and go back to admiring the woodwork.

escape.generic: The jury box stayed empty, the case went in a drawer marked 'later', and somewhere out there a very junior lawyer is telling the furniture-restoration story at parties and leaving out the ending.

byAccused.A: Arthur was led out still mid-backswing, gavel confiscated at the door, insisting to the last that a judge is entitled to his exercise, while the real culprit walked past the evidence room without breaking stride.
byAccused.B: Benjamin never did get the seat, and never will now — the woman he'd spent the day glaring at kept it, flask and all, while the actual killer strolled out through the gallery he'd been so busy guarding.
byAccused.C: Camila's own verdict on being arrested was 'I queued since six for this,' repeated twice more on the way out, sketchbook confiscated as evidence of nothing at all, while the true culprit never made it onto a single page of it.
byAccused.D: Daisy was marched off the Prosecution carpet mid-sentence, insisting at full volume that she'd never once stepped off it — which was true, and which the real killer, three rooms over and perfectly audible, had been quietly grateful for.
byAccused.E: Eliza's account of her sister's wedding never did get its ending, cut off by a pair of handcuffs at minute forty-one, and somewhere across town a bride is still wondering what happened at the reception while the real killer made it home for dinner.
byAccused.G: The other guards agreed Graham definitely hadn't been watching the monitors, which they took as proof of guilt rather than of wildebeest, and let the real killer walk right past the desk he was meant to be minding.
byAccused.H: The county now believes, on no evidence beyond a raised voice near a filing cabinet, that Howard's decade-old boundary dispute was somehow the motive here, and nobody has yet corrected them — least of all the real killer.
